implementation_notes: Scala's Predef offers the closest mainstream analogue of design by contract: require(cond) throws IllegalArgumentException and blames the caller, assert(cond) throws AssertionError for internal predicates, and ensuring(cond) attaches a postcondition to the result of an expression - the documented example reads like Eiffel's require/ensure pair. assert, assume and ensuring are annotated @elidable, so scalac -Xdisable-assertions (or -Xelide-below above ASSERTION) removes them from the bytecode, while require is never elided. Immutable case classes with smart constructors keep most invariants in the constructor, which is where require belongs.
pitfalls: assert, assume and ensuring are elidable with -Xdisable-assertions while require is not: choose the function by whether the check must survive production builds.
The message argument is by-name and only evaluated on failure, but the condition itself is evaluated eagerly, so costly predicates cost on every successful call.
ensuring on a Unit method has no result to inspect; postconditions need a value-returning expression to attach to.
